schools.summary: Gill weighs 'call now' as calling upon God (good advice, but Eliphaz insinuates it would be vain), or calling for an oracle, or calling over the catalogue of good men to find one so dealt with.
Henry hears a motion to arbitration: Eliphaz lets Job choose the arbitrators, claiming the communis sensus fidelium, the unanimous vote of the faithful, on his side.

Clarke takes it as strong irony and reads 'the saints' as the holy ones (kedoshim), angels or beings dependent on God to whom prayer is vain; Wesley bids Job call the saints by name, sure not one child of God will defend his expostulations.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'to whom of the holy ones wilt thou turn?' and fix the 'holy ones' as the angels (as in Ps. 89); Ellicott marks the tone turning personal, insinuating Job 'unwise' and 'silly.'

debates.question: Who are the 'saints' / 'holy ones' to whom Job is bidden turn?

sides.position: godly men, the faithful whose verdict Eliphaz claims
the angels, the heavenly holy ones, to whom no cry can avail

schools.summary: Gill defines the 'foolish' as a wicked man void of divine knowledge, and allows the wrath to be either the Lord's judgment (Targum) or the man's own passion rising till it kills him.
Henry lays the weight on the man's own passion — his wrath a fire in his bones, envy the rottenness of the bones — so that quarrelling with God, Job does himself the greatest mischief.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'he is a fool who is destroyed by complaining, and envy slays the simple one,' binding the death to Job's own fretting under the oracle that God is absolutely just.

Clarke reads it as a maxim — God's wrath is manifested only against the wicked, so were Job not such God would not contend with him; Wesley: a man's wrath preys on his spirit and provokes God to cut him off.

sides.position: God's kindled wrath and judgment (the Targum's 'wrath of the Lord')
the man's own passion, complaining, and envy consuming him

schools.summary: Gill sees Eliphaz granting that the wicked prosper 'for a while' to obviate the objection to his thesis, but insisting they soon pass away with their substance.
Henry reads 'taking root' as the false security of the worldly, and 'cursed' as prognostication, not prayer — Eliphaz foresaw their ruin as one who understood their end in the sanctuary.
Clarke: 'I ventured to pronounce their doom, for in God's providence it was inevitable'; Wesley glosses foolish, root, suddenly, and 'cursed' (I saw by the event he was accursed of God).
Ellicott renders 'I cursed' as 'I declared distinctly his lot would be as follows,' and names the sting — the insinuation of secret unsoundness in Job, the guilty victim of a just judge.
Gill takes the children as far from outward, spiritual, and eternal safety, treading in their fathers' steps under the visited iniquity.
Clarke fixes 'crushed in the gate' to the tribunal at the city gate (Targum: the gate of hell at the great judgment); Wesley says Eliphaz plainly glances at the death of Job's children.
Ellicott proposes 'they crush one another' — internal rivalries and dissensions bringing them to ruin, the house divided against itself.
Henry reads the literal picture — the gate or doorway falling heaviest on them, none to deliver — with the common application to families crushed by justice or oppression.

debates.question: What is meant by 'crushed in the gate'?

sides.position: crushed at the tribunal / court of justice sitting in the city gate
they crush one another through their own dissensions
crushed under a falling house, glancing at Job's own children

schools.summary: Gill reads the foolish rich man's harvest eaten by his hungry heirs or the poor he oppressed, and reports Sephorno's turn that the wicked eats his own harvest yet is unsatisfied.

Clarke sees possessions pillaged by desert banditti and reads 'robber' as 'the thirsty' (tsammim) against 'the hungry'; Wesley makes 'the hungry Sabeans eat it up,' taken from the fields in spite of danger.

Ellicott takes the wicked man himself as subject, eating his scant harvest famishing from among thorns; 'robber' perhaps 'a trap,' and old versions read 'the thirsty swallow up' to complete the parallelism.

debates.question: Is the last spoiler 'the robber' or 'the thirsty'?

sides.position: 'the robber,' as the received text reads
'the thirsty' (tsammim), for the parallel with 'the hungry'

schools.summary: Gill reads the particle as 'for,' making affliction come not from the creatures but from God for sin; the word also signifies iniquity, which Aben Ezra and others take of moral, not natural, evil.

Henry gives both readings — affliction comes not by chance but by God's counsel, and 'sin comes not out of the dust,' so blame not soil or stars but ourselves; the one bids us be patient, the other penitent.
Clarke drives it at Job: 'if there were not an adequate cause, thou couldst not be so grievously afflicted' — trouble comes from God's justice on offending man, not from natural causes.

debates.question: Does the verse say 'affliction' or 'sin/iniquity' does not spring from the ground?

sides.position: affliction/trouble — it comes not by chance but from God
sin/iniquity — blame not the soil or stars but yourself (the word's moral sense)

themes: the double sense of the word

schools.summary: Gill takes 'born unto trouble' as born by God's appointment for sin, trouble springing from original corruption, the fountain of all bodily and mental evil and death.
Henry: man is brought to trouble not as man but as sinful man; actual transgressions are the sparks that fly out of the furnace of original corruption, so troubles rise as thick as sparks.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the received rendering, reading the whole as designed to bring down man's haughtiness.

Clarke breaks with the rest, rendering 'born to labour' and 'the sons of the coal lift up their flight' — bold men who rise above trials (with Coverdale's 'the byrde for to fle'); Wesley keeps the traditional sparks of fire flying upward.

debates.question: What is meant by 'as the sparks fly upward'?

sides.position: kindled sparks/flames rising, an image of man's inborn trouble
'the sons of the flame lift up their flight' — bold men who rise above trials (or Coverdale's bird)

schools.summary: Gill hears the emphatic Hebrew as Eliphaz describing his own practice under affliction — 'I do seek unto God' — proposed for Job's imitation, with submission and confession.
Henry hears 'surely I would' as a tacit reproof, yet good counsel: by prayer we fetch in grace, by patience we commit our cause — 'Is any afflicted? let him pray; it is a salve for every sore.'
Clarke: 'were I in your place, I would apply to my Maker and confidently commit my cause to him'; Wesley: seek by prayer, humiliation, and submission, imploring pardon and favour.

debates.question: Is Eliphaz stating his own practice or what he would do in Job's place?

sides.position: his own practice under affliction ('I do seek')
what he would do were he in Job's condition ('I would seek')

schools.summary: Gill sorts the 'great things' into creation, providence, and above all grace — the covenant, redemption, and the new heart — as encouragement to seek the Lord.
Henry expounds the three epithets — unsearchable, numberless, marvellous — both to rebuke Job's quarrelling with a God above judgment and to encourage him to seek One to whom such power belongs.

Clarke: no work too deep for his counsel or too great for his power; Wesley: Eliphaz sets out God's infinite perfection to show the disproportion between God and Job and convince him of his bold speaking.
Gill widens the gift to the whole earth against the Targum's Israel-only reading — a free gift on godly and ungodly alike, which no Gentile vanity can give.

Clarke keeps the Chaldee's turn (rain on Israel, waters on the provinces), tied to Matt. 5:45, and reads 'fields' (chutsoth) as the tilled ridges each watered; Wesley finds the wonder in the rising and hanging of the rain.
Henry: 'he gives rain' stands for all common providence — a great work of power and goodness we reckon little only because it is common.

debates.question: Is the rain given on the whole earth or on the land of Israel?

sides.position: upon the whole earth, on godly and ungodly alike
upon the land of Israel (the Targum's reading)

themes: a great work in a little thing

schools.summary: Gill gives the agricultural sense first — husbandmen in low circumstances raised to good estates by the rain that makes their lands fruitful.
Clarke: God's impartial bounty waters the poor man's land as well as the rich, setting him on a level with the lords of the soil; Wesley: 'he setteth up,' able to raise Job from his greatest depths.
Ellicott draws the doctrine that man's exaltation must come from God, not his own strivings, ranging it with Hannah's song and the psalms of reversal.
Henry hears the humble and mourning exalted and made safe, and binds the verse to Mary's song of the proud scattered and the low degree raised (Luke 1:51-53).

debates.question: Are the 'low' those literally raised by the rain, or the humble whom God exalts?

sides.position: husbandmen in low estate raised by the fruitful rain
the humble, lowly, and mourning whom God exalts

schools.summary: Gill records the minority reading that the subject is the rain (which disappoints those who hoard corn in drought), and the Targum's application to the Egyptians, before the plain sense of God disappointing the wily.
Clarke gathers the sweep of particular providence ever counterworking the plots of the wicked, breaking their machinery so their hands cannot perform.
Ellicott tightens the clause: their hands 'can do nothing that is sound or of worth,' accomplishing nothing effectual.
Henry stages it in history — the froward crafty as the serpent's seed, their plots (Ahithophel, Sanballat, Haman) baffled by the supreme power that overrules them.

debates.question: Is the subject that disappoints the crafty 'He' (God) or 'it' (the rain)?

sides.position: God, whose providence overrules the crafty
the rain, which disappoints those who hoard corn

schools.summary: Gill: crafty men wise in their own conceit are snared in their own schemes — Haman on his gallows, Joseph's brethren fulfilling by selling him the dreams they meant to defeat.
Ellicott records Paul's citation of the verse in 1 Cor. 3:19 and glosses 'froward' as crooked (the root of Naphtali); Keil and Delitzsch render 'the counsel of the cunning is thrown down.'

Clarke turns it into the universal adage that the pit-digger falls in, quoting Lucretius; Wesley reads 'the froward' as wrestlers who wind every way yet are carried headlong by their own precipitation.
Henry: what enemies designed for the church's ruin turns to their own, and notes the apostle quotes the verse to show the heathen learned befooled by their own philosophy.

themes: the wise taken in their craftiness

schools.summary: Gill reads the darkness as judicial blindness in things most plain, the greatest politicians blundering, or their counsels defeated in the meridian of their glory.
Clarke: God confounds them so they act in noonday as if the sun were extinct; Wesley reads the darkness as ignorance and error, groping like blind men, not knowing what to do.
Ellicott hears a possible allusion to the Egyptian plague of darkness (Exod. 10:21) as a note of date, comparing Isaiah 59:10 — one of many hints of acquaintance with the Pentateuch.
Henry: when God infatuates men they are perplexed in the plainest things, running into darkness by the violence of their own counsels.

outliers.note: Hears in 'darkness in the daytime' a possible echo of the Egyptian plague of darkness (Exod. 10:21), taking it as a slight indication of the book's acquaintance with the Pentateuch and of its date.

schools.summary: Gill reads the poor literally — the butt of the crafty, helpless and friendless, whom God takes notice of and saves.
Clarke finds 'from the sword, from their mouth' harsh, and prefers with eleven MSS and the versions 'from the sword of their mouth,' saving the poor from the hand of the mighty.
Ellicott treats the syntax as a nicety but lifts the wonder: the Lord conceived as the Saviour, and the Saviour of them who have no saviour — an idea characteristic of the sacred writings.
Henry: God protects the poor who commit themselves to him, saving them from the mouth that speaks hard things and the hand that does them, for he can tie the tongue and wither the hand.

debates.question: How is the phrase 'from the sword, from their mouth' to be read?

sides.position: three deliverances — from sword, from mouth, from the mighty (received text)
'from the sword of their mouth' (with the manuscripts and versions)

themes: the Saviour of them who have no saviour

schools.summary: Gill lets the poor reason from what he sees and from past deliverance to a comfortable hope, applying it also to the spiritually poor who hope for safety in Christ.

Clarke fixes 'the poor' (dal) as the wasted man who hopes because he sees what God is wont to do, so the mouth of impiety is stopped; Wesley: iniquity, the wicked, silenced and ensnared in their own snares.
Ellicott anchors 'iniquity stoppeth her mouth' in its echo of Psalm 107:42.
Henry draws the two effects: weak saints comforted with hope, and daring sinners confounded, iniquity stopping her mouth and owning the justice of God.
Gill distinguishes a father's correction from a judge's condemnation — God correcting by word, ministers, Spirit, and afflictive providence, to bring to repentance.

Henry expounds the paradox — happy because afflicted, correction weaning the heart from the world — and notes that as Paul quoted v.13 as Scripture and this command binds us, the promises may be received as divine.

Ellicott judges the verse probably the original of Prov. 3:12 (quoted in Heb. 12:5), and the only place in Job with the Psalter's first word 'happy'; Keil and Delitzsch render 'whom Eloah correcteth' and mark the speech turning persuasive.

Clarke notes 'behold' wanting in several MSS and appeals to the Father of spirits who chastens that we may share his holiness (Heb. 12:5); Wesley hears the Hebrew plural 'blessednesses' as proof the ancients held the hope of everlasting blessedness.

themes: happy is the man God correcteth
a father's chastening not a judge's
the source of Prov. 3:12 and Heb. 12:5

schools.summary: Gill reads it concessively — 'though he maketh sore, yet he bindeth up' — with the surgeon who probes to open the wound before laying on the plaster, in body and in spirit.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'He woundeth, and He also bindeth up; He bruiseth, and His hands make whole'; Ellicott owns the sentiment obvious yet coming home in sorrow with a power boundless because Divine.
Clarke prizes Coverdale's nervous rendering: 'though he make a wounde, he giveth a medicyne agayne; though he smyte, his honde maketh whole agayne.'
Henry: God's method is first to wound then to heal, binding up by the Spirit's consolations the wounds his providence made — 'the hand that inflicts the wound applies the cure.'

themes: he maketh sore and bindeth up

schools.summary: Gill makes the deliverance conditional on seeking God and not despising the chastening, six and seven being a certain number for an uncertain.

Clarke: six and seven for many — God rids of all troubles at once, and he who delivered before will not deny help now; Wesley applies it directly to Job, promising a good issue out of great and many troubles.
Ellicott marks the numerical figure as characteristic of the Proverbs, and hears bitter irony, since evil was at that moment emphatically touching Job.
Henry: as troubles recur, deliverances are repeated, former rescues being earnests of more; 'no evil shall touch thee' means the sting is taken out.

outliers.note: Feels the bitter irony that the promise 'in seven there shall no evil touch thee' is spoken to a man whom evil was, at that very moment, emphatically touching.

schools.summary: Gill reads God's special care in extremity — his own not starved in famine, as food was found for the patriarchs, God sometimes working wonders for his needy.

Clarke keeps the Chaldee's Egypt-and-Amalek reading; Wesley exposes Eliphaz's premise that great afflictions are the certain evidence of wickedness and great deliverances the sure fruit of repentance.
Ellicott presses the verb — 'he hath redeemed thee' — an appeal to Job's own past experience as a ground of hope.
Henry: when desolating judgments are abroad the godly are under special protection — kept alive in famine, redeemed from the sword that has no power but from above.

debates.question: Is the redemption a future promise or an appeal to Job's past?

sides.position: future — 'he shall redeem thee' from famine and sword
past — 'he hath redeemed thee,' an appeal to Job's experience

outliers.note: Names the flawed premise driving Eliphaz's confidence — that great afflictions are certain evidence of wickedness, and great deliverances the infallible fruit of repentance — which, applied to Job, was false.

schools.summary: Gill takes the scourge of the tongue as the slanders of wicked men (Jarchi: Satan the accuser), from which God hides his people by restraining tongues or discrediting the slander.
Clarke pours out the catalogue of the tongue's sins — that member 'a world of fire kindled from the nethermost hell' — and bids such confidence in God as fears not even death before destruction.
Ellicott ties the fear here to the language of v.15, knitting the paragraph together.
Henry: none, even the innocent, can secure themselves from calumny, but God can hide him so it neither disturbs his peace nor blemishes his name, restraining the remainder of wrath.

themes: hid from the scourge of the tongue

schools.summary: Gill guards the laughter from scorn — not deriding God's judgments but reckoning oneself safe amid them, cheerful in trust, like a man in a good harbour laughing at the storm (cf. Hab. 3:17).
Clarke reads the strongest security (with the Targum's Sihon and Og); Wesley: a laughter of joy and triumph from confidence in God's watchful providence.
Ellicott renders the second clause literally, 'and of the beasts of the earth be not thou afraid,' keeping its imperative force.
Henry lifts it to triumph in God over the world's grievances, as Paul laughed at destruction — 'O death, where is thy sting?' — being more than conquerors (Rom. 8:35).

themes: the laughter of trust not scorn

schools.summary: Gill takes literal field-stones at truce — no hurt walking among them, no hindrance to crops, useful as landmarks — and records Pineda's 'Scopelism,' the Arabian custom of laying stones to threaten a field.

Clarke sets out Good's emendation 'sons of the field' (rejected), the Chaldee's covenant on tables of stone, and his own reading of strongholds and chieftains turned confederate ('the castels in the londe'); Wesley calls it a bold metaphor of a covenant with all the creatures.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain construction — the man in league with the field-stones and at peace with the beasts.
Henry gives the theology: at peace with God, a man is in covenant with the whole creation, for 'a reconciled God reconciles all things' (cf. Hos. 2:18).

debates.question: What are the 'stones of the field' with which the man is in league?

sides.position: literal field-stones at truce, doing no hurt
strongholds and neighbouring chieftains turned confederate
an emended 'sons/produce of the field'

outliers.note: Reads the 'stones of the field' not as literal stones but as the rocks and strongholds where chieftains and banditti dwelt, now made confederate with the man instead of preying on him like the Sabeans.

themes: a reconciled God reconciles all things

schools.summary: Gill takes the 'tabernacle' as the dwelling-house built tent-wise (as the patriarchs') including the household, promised peace if the man behave aright under God's hand.

Clarke distinguishes ohel (movable tent) from naveh (permanent dwelling) and reads 'shalt not sin' (chata, to miss the mark) as 'thou shalt make no mistake,' the Arab chiefs being attacked in their absence.
Ellicott: the word 'sin' means to miss the mark (Judg. 20:16), so 'thou shalt visit thy dwelling and miss nothing,' since a promise of not sinning ill-suits visiting the fold.
Henry keeps the moral sense — 'peace is thy tabernacle,' and 'thou shalt not sin' or wander like Cain — finding in the 'visiting' the wisdom and grace to govern a household without sin.

debates.question: Does the last clause mean 'thou shalt not sin' or 'thou shalt miss nothing'?

sides.position: moral — thou shalt not sin, nor wander like a fugitive
'miss nothing' / make no mistake (chata = to miss the mark)

themes: not sin or miss the mark

schools.summary: Gill reads 'thy seed' of the man's children (with Bar Tzemach), great in worldly things or in number, a multitude of children a great temporal blessing.

Keil and Delitzsch link the verse to Ps. 72:16 and note the word for 'offspring' found only in Isaiah and Job; Ellicott reads 'great' as 'numerous' and owns the promise beautiful yet vitiated by not corresponding to facts — Job's own case the crucial instance.
Clarke: 'thou shalt have a numerous and permanent issue'; Wesley grounds the knowing in God's promises and the Spirit's impressions, confirmed by experience.
Henry feels the tenderness toward Job, who had lost all his children — if he return to God his family shall be built up again, flourishing as the grass.

outliers.note: Grants the description of guaranteed increase a beautiful picture of faith's security, yet 'vitiated by its want of strict correspondence with facts,' Job's own emptied house being the crucial counter-instance the friends could not solve.

themes: the promise that broke on Job's case

schools.summary: Gill figures the grave as man's long home, and reads coming to it 'in a full age' as a willingness to die, giving up the ghost cheerfully, unlike those whose souls are required against their will.
Clarke reads a death in season, buried 'like a wholesome seed' to rise into an eternal spring; Wesley: a mature but vigorous old age, willing and seasonable, ripe for God.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the rare word as the maturity of old age, set against the sheaves brought to the threshing-floor; Ellicott hears a contrast of going down to the grave and up to the barn — the grave a passage to a higher life (2 Tim. 4:8).

themes: the grave in a full age
the shock of corn in its season
the grave as passage to a higher life

schools.summary: Gill: Eliphaz seals his oration by claiming the shared sentiment of his friends and the fruit of laborious inquiry into the records of former times, bidding Job lay it to heart.

Clarke calls it the sum of established maxims that universal experience supports — 'wise saws and ancient instances' — yet miserably perverted in their application to Job; Wesley: no rash conceit but the fruit of deep consideration and long experience, to be known for oneself.
Keil and Delitzsch mark the close as an epimythion tacked to the whole speech; Ellicott fastens on the boastful confidence 'which is so hard to bear' — 'This is mine: take it to thyself.'

themes: we have searched it, so it is
